opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes from caring about them. When I see a young researcher with real talent, the worst thing I can do is be polite and say "looks good." That doesn't help anyone. If the problem isn't important, or the experiments don't actually support the claim, or the idea is just a small increment on something that already exists, I'd rather they hear it from me in a meeting than from reviewers six months later, or worse, realize after two years that they spent their best time on the wrong problem.

Early in a career, time is the most precious resource. The habits you form, how you pick problems, how honest you are with your own results, how high your bar is, stay with you for a long time. So when I'm critical, I'm usually pushing on a few things: Is this problem worth solving? If it works, what changes? Are you fooling yourself anywhere? I try to be direct about the work, never about the person.

I was lucky to have mentors who were very honest with me, and sometimes it hurt, but looking back those were the conversations that shaped me most. So I see it as passing that on. Being critical is a form of respect. It means I think you're capable of doing something much better, and I'm taking your work seriously enough to argue with it.

r001.rationale: The response says Liu is critical because he sees talented young researchers as capable of doing much better. It does not connect that potential to needing only a little more polish.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes from a sense of responsibility, honestly. When I was a young researcher, the people who helped me the most were not the ones who told me my work was great. They were the ones who told me, very directly, where it was weak. At the time it didn't feel good. But looking back, that's what made me a better researcher.

So when I see a young person present work, and there's a flaw in the experimental setup, or the claim is bigger than the evidence, or they're comparing against a baseline that's not really fair, I feel I owe it to them to say so. If I just nod and say "nice work," I'm being polite, but I'm not being useful. And in research, being useful matters more than being polite.

There's also a second reason, which is about the field itself. Right now, especially in generative AI, there's so much excitement, so much money, so much hype. It's very easy for a young researcher to get rewarded for a flashy demo rather than for careful science. If senior people don't push back, the incentives drift in the wrong direction. Somebody has to hold the bar.

But I want to be clear about one thing. Being critical of the work is not the same as being critical of the person. When I push on a paper, I try to focus on the technical question: does this claim hold, is this comparison fair, what would convince me. I'm not trying to make anyone feel small. Actually, I think if you take the time to criticize someone's work seriously, that's a form of respect. It means you believe they can do better. The work I don't bother to comment on is usually the work I don't think is going anywhere.

And of course, I expect the same in return. If my team's work has a problem, I want to hear it. That's how the whole thing is supposed to function.

r001.rationale: The response says criticism reflects respect and that young researchers can do better, but it does not identify their unrealized potential to improve substantially with a little more polish as what prompts him to speak up.

astra-6.text: I think it’s important to be honest with young researchers. If I see a weakness in the work, I want to discuss it rather than just say, “Good job.” The goal is to help them ask sharper questions and make the work stronger. But I also have to be open to being wrong. Criticism should start a conversation, not shut one down.

r001.rationale: The response says criticism can help strengthen young researchers’ work, but it does not identify their unrealized potential to do substantially better with a little more polish as the reason Liu speaks up.

sol-6.1.text: I think speaking up is part of taking someone’s work seriously. If I see a weakness in the reasoning or a claim that isn’t supported, I want to explain it clearly so the researcher has something useful to work with. But the criticism should stay focused on the work. Young researchers need room to try things and make mistakes, and I should be willing to listen if I’ve misunderstood what they’re doing.

r001.rationale: The response says criticism can help researchers address weaknesses and emphasizes room to make mistakes, but it does not identify unrealized potential or the belief that a little more polish could make their work substantially better as the reason for speaking up.
